DURBAN TOXIC FUMES & SMOKE SCREENS

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Did the company behind the torched chemical plant that was a blaze for more than week tick all the boxes when it came to environmental approvals and permits – a community at risk is furious and dem

Unique Selling Point:
** FOOTAGE AVAILABLE
** GREAT NARRITIVE WITH LOCAL RESIDENTS THAT ARE THE TYPICAL CB VIEWERS

Summary:
The arson attack on the United Phosphorus Limited (UPL)Chemical factory is the biggest environmental disaster arising from the KZN unrest. The building north of Durban burned for days, taking firefighters more than a week to douse the flames - the damage is not confined to the facility.

Smoke blanketed the north of Durban and rivers, lagoons and beaches all the way up to the North Coast were contaminated. The fire was finally extinguished by 5pm on Thursday.

Unanswered questions around the approval of the factory that opened in April this year have local residents and environmental activists up in arms as the extent of the damage to the environment and the human life is yet to be determined.


Further information:
The UPL warehouse in Cornubia, which housed 1600 hazardous herbicides, fungicides and pesticides, was targeted Monday 12 July by looters.

The Indian multinational pesticide company United Phosphorus Limited (UPL)’s Chemical Plant in Cornubia, Durban is situated near the uMhlanga lagoon and the Ohlanga River, which feeds into the Indian Ocean.

ACCORDING TO ETHEKWINI MUNICIPALITY UPL NEVER APPLIED FOR A PERMIT TO STORE HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS THAT HAD AFFECTED AIR AND WATER.

Sabelo Ngcobo, director for impact management and coastal management at the provincial level, responding to a question about the environmental impact assessment, said one developer for the area had applied for everything to be undertaken.

"It was not specific to UPL. It was registered for residential, logistics, commercial and light industrial use. UPL was authorised within that authority. We still need to determine whether they were compliant."

WHAT WENT UP IN FLAME
The plant housed hundreds of hazardous herbicides, fungicides and pesticides. It only opened it’s doors at this site in April 2021 – just four months before the blaze. It took firefighters more than a week to douse the flames and the damage was not confined to the facility.

A complete list of the volume and types of pesticides and other poisonous products that were set on fire has yet to be disclosed publicly as this might “create unnecessary anxiety”, the company suggested earlier this week.

Though it remains unclear what exactly was in the warehouse at the time of the fire, the Indian agrochemicals chemicals giant UPL markets a wide range of highly toxic formulations on its South African website including 52 insecticides, 124 herbicides, 43 fungicides, rat poison, fumigants and other poisonous compounds — notably 2,4-D, glyphosate, paraquat, chlorophenoxy, triclopyrbutoxy ethel esters, atrazine, carbofuran, cyanamide and chlorpyrifos.

eThekwini Fire Department Divisional Commander Bruce de Gier noted that the warehouse caved in and collapsed within the space of about an hour after a massive fireball explosion tore through the roof of the warehouse, ripping the overhead sprinkler systems and water pipes out of the walls and roof.

The remains of smouldering chemical drums and canisters were now covered by tons of metal sheeting, steel beams, brick and concrete debris, making it impossible to douse the fire completely. “The fireball went through the roof in front of our eyes. The building was completely destroyed. It looks like Hiroshima inside there now.”

KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department's Sphume Nowele described the levels of toxicity after the chemical spillage and air pollution in parts of the province: “It is serious, and it should not be underestimated in any way.”

BUT WAS THE PLANT DODGE TO START WITH?
Further concerns have also been raised about why a major storage facility housing hazardous and toxic chemicals did not have bunding to contain the deadly overflow into the environment. Bunds are similar to large concrete moats that are designed to capture and contain effluent overflow and pollution – even in the event of heavy rainfall and the large volumes of water often used to fight fires.

Senior manager for pollution control in eThekwini Metro, Bruce Dale, said there was also no Major Hazard Installation (MHI). In occupational health terms, an MHI ensures the quantity of any substance that has the potential to cause a major incident is kept.

"Unfortunately, it does not appear there was any Major Hazard Installation application made and unfortunately local government, we are not aware and it was not brought to our attention that there was a storage facility there.

"If it was brought to our attention, we know there are sensitive receptors downstream including the sea, estuary and shopping centres. Unfortunately, we are not aware of any MHI application otherwise they would have brought it to the attention of the municipality and we would have had to look at mitigation measures to prevent any explosions or impact on the environment in terms of air quality and water quality impacts."

It appears that UPL does not have an approved Environmental Management Plan in place, as it has submitted a plan but has not received approval yet – by the company’s own admittance – “the plan became somewhat academic due to the extraordinary circumstances which could not have been foreseen, notably the civil unrest which resulted in the looting and arson and barricading of access routes which resulted in the long delay in the fire department and other response services being able to access the site.”

NOTE! THE PLANT OPENED 4 MONTHS BEFORE THE LOOTING

Siphumelele Nowele, chief director of environmental management at the department, said that if it was deliberately hidden from them that highly toxic substances were stored there, there were processes to follow that could lead to criminal action.
"But we can't jump to that point until we know."

From a waste management point of view, because the kind of chemicals at UPL were highly hazardous, they should not be disposed of at a landfill site without provincial consent.

ENVIRONMENTAL AND HEALTH IMPACTS
The pollution from the days-long burning fire at the UPL chemical plant resulted in dead fish washing ashore because of toxins from the Umhlanga lagoon.

While the KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department has started running tests and evaluating the damage to the environment, an additional team of specialists in aquatic systems, epidemiology, waste and pollution as well as oceans and coasts compliance will provide support.

BEACHES & BUSINESSES CLOSED
Beaches in the vicinity remain closed to the public and while some businesses are desperate to reopen, they’ve been advised that this was not safe, as the damage and its costs were evaluated.

Oceanographer Lisa Gaustella estimates that the lagoon would take “maybe a year or two” to recover, starting with organisms that live there and in the ocean.“In the upper reaches, smaller animals like frogs, which are a good indicator of wetland health, will take longer.”

HEALTH IMPACT
There had been "numerous complaints" through emergency services regarding air quality.

Residents in both nearby residential estates and informal settlements have been affected. Some people have evacuated their homes; others have had to undergo medical treatment for respiratory problems and nausea.
** HAVE A LONG LIST OF CASE STUDIES WILLING TO GO ON CAMERA

Reggie Govender, a doctor based in Somerset Park, confirmed “About five patients a day have been coming in for the past week - it has mainly affected chronic sinusitis and asthmatic patients but even people without these are also complaining,”
Rory Macpherson, the local councillor for Mount Edgecombe/Umhlanga who visited the beach near the Ohlanga River mouth said “This estuary is dead, dead, dead … and the sea and coastline have also been poisoned”.
Macpherson also drove to Cornubia earlier last week and discovered that polluted bright blue water was still flowing out of a broken stormwater drain some distance from the warehouse alongside a stream that leads into the Ohlanga River.
Local civil society groups have also issued an “urgent but unofficial public health warning” cautioning people in the vicinity to stay indoors and to consider moving vulnerable people out of the area for the next few days.
“As far as is possible, stay indoors as much as you can, with windows closed, particularly if your home is in the direction of the chemical plume. If you, your child, or elderly people with chronic chest and heart disease live in the area of the smoke, and it is at all possible to stay with relatives outside the area for the next few days, then it is advisable to do so,” according to a press statement signed by among others, Prof Rajen Naidoo, head of Occupational and Environmental Health at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
According to UPL, Verdoorn had indicated that some of the herbicides, such as acetochlor, metolachlor, phenoxy carboxylic acids (2,4-D, MCPA and benzoic acids, or dicamba) may not have burnt out completely:
“Two pyrethroids — alpha-cypermethrin and lambda-cyhalothrin — which are dermal, eye and respiratory tract irritants may have been present in the smoke. These chemicals were suspended in the atmosphere and have precipitated since the fire, more noticeably during the late night and early hours of the morning, resulting in an acrid smell.
“Combined with the smoke inhalation, this may cause drying out of the mucous membranes in the nasal tract and some mild bleeding, especially when blowing the nose. It may also cause discomfort in the oesophagus and trachea.
“However as the fire is being doused, the release of these substances into the atmosphere diminishes. This can be expected to dissipate rapidly due to normal air movement and precipitation.
SPECIALIST TESTING UNDERWAY
Specialists in marine biology, water, air, chemicals, estuaries and others were still awaiting test results to determine the severity of the pollution.

Air pollution also remains a major concern, as firefighters continue to douse the still smouldering debris. A lot of the gases that people have been breathing in there have been very high in sulphur, that could affect, particularly, people with respiratory illnesses.

KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department's Sphume Nowele said - “We are going to be getting those results so that we can make informed decisions in terms of what happens moving forward.”

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: The violent riots and looting that ripped through KwaZulu Natal in July, has also triggered extensive environmental damage, following the arson attack on the United Phosphorus Limited, or UPL Chemical warehouse in Cornubia, north of Durban.

LINK: IT’S THE BIGGEST ECOLOGICAL DISASTER TO COME OUT OF THE UNPRECEDENTED KZN UNREST. THE SITE WAS ABLAZE FOR 9 DAYS , COVERING THE SURROUNDING AREA IN A THICK BLACK CLOUD OF SMOKE.

VO: Babalo Masiphula lives in the informal settlement of Blackburn.

BABALO: you can't just breathe bread and as normal as you always it because it's affecting you or your chest

VO: He recalls the air pollution was most intense at night, With shacks erected less than 2km from the site.

Specialist Anesthesiologist, Dr. Mitha Ramnarain lives about 5 kilometers from the site in Mount Edgecombe. She felt anxious as the clouds of airborne chemicals lingered over her home with ash falling from the sky - as a precaution she kept her children indoors.

MITHA: it smelt quite chemical in nature. It was acrid. It was malodorous, would probably be a euphemistic way to describe the odor. It was it smelled like something was going to choke me.

VO: UPL, an Indian multinational pesticide and agro-chemicals company – opened Cornubia warehouse in April. It is said to have stored herbicides, pesticide and fungicides – and believed to have contained more than 1500 chemicals that UPL say are overwhelmingly water-based.

Fire fighting efforts were hampered with the ongoing unrest straining resources and delaying accessibility to the fire.

The roof and surrounding walls collapsed in the intense heat , covering much of the products in metal sheeting and debris. The water used to douse the raging flames, mixed with the exposed chemicals - spilled into the surrounding environment.

The effects could be seen in the river, the lagoon, estuary and on the beaches – the water turned a bright turquoise colour and dead fish washed up in affected areas. Beaches were closed, and Blackburn residents were advised not to use the water.

BABALO: The water is very bad even now, it's still very bad. //uh, during that week, the water will have changed the color into green.

VO: Steven Weerts is a specialist estuarine and marine ecologist.

MAC: What did you see the impact of the UPL spill has had? How bad is it?
STEVEN: it has pretty much decimated all the aquatic life in that system.

VO: Scores of dead marine life were cleared by cleaning companies. These teams are still working on the affected water in the Blackburn area.

STEVEN: Those chemical compounds. are designed for agricultural purposes to weed out unwanted things. So they are typically toxic to some elements of wildlife. And obviously in extreme toxicity there's going to be human impact.

VO: Residents like, Dr. Ramnarain, were surprised to find out that a chemical storage facility was in such close proximity to residential areas.

MITHA: we didn't even know such a factory existed having a chemical warehouse so close to so many conservancies in our area and so many residents, have just left lots of people with no choices and the environment with no choice

VO: UPL believes it was appropriately zoned and said in a press release that “the designed fire and containment systems were more than adequate, in ordinary circumstances, to have enabled the facility and the relevant authorities to contain a fire and any associated spillage of product”.
Government and City Officials, however, revealed at a press conference not all boxes were ticked by UPL related to approvals and permitting.
The onus is on the facility to check what regulations are applicable in order to comply with the laws of that area.
UPSOUND PRESS CONFERENCE - BRUCE DALE, SENIOR MANAGER: Ethekwini Municipality
25:36 “They were not in possession of a Scheduled Trade Permit. They did trigger activity, a listing activity in terms of the bylaws. So it's notable there was an aggregation, all of those scheduled activities.”

VO: UPL BELIEVES IT WAS FIT FOR PURPOSE.

The KZN Provincial Government disclosed that a “specific” environmental impact assessment wasn’t done for the UPL operation. Only an “integrated environmental assessment” was approved for the entire mixed-use development .

In terms of a clause in the environmental authorisation a separate EIA would ONLY be required for facilities with storage and handling of dangerous goods that exceed 80m3 in capacity. It’s unclear whether UPL fell into that category or not.

The UPL press statement said the company was advised that it did not trigger an environmental assessment under NEMA regulations and that advice has since been confirmed by its legal consultants.

VO: The Greater Cornubia mixed-use development project was part of a special national government investment initiative, aimed at attracting investors by prioritizing and fast tracking the normal regulatory processes.

Bobby Peek from the environmental justice organisation, GroundWork, believes this created a loophole for companies to bypass some regulations that are intended to prevent harm to human health and the environment.

BOBBY: in a normal legal process.. there would have been an emergency response system created for those that could have been impacted upon if something went wrong at this facility. None of that took place.

VO: South African legislation ensures the rights of citizens to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being is protected, explains Professor of Law, Tracy-Lynn Field.

TRACY: // The problem with deciding whether those laws apply is that we don't know. We haven't been given the information. The company has not disclosed the exact chemicals and the quantities that were available on that site.

VO: Initially, even the authorities were not given a complete inventory by UPL , subsequently it has been supplied, but not made public.

TRACY: What would be a reasonable and justifiable limitation of the right to information in this instance? // I can't think of a good reason.

LINK: GROUNDWORK HAS SEEN THE INVENTORY OF SOME OF THE CHEMICALS THAT WERE STORED AT THE WAREHOUSE. AND OF THOSE 5 ARE CLASSIFIED AS HIGHLY HAZARDOUS PESTICIDES BY THE United Nations BODIES THAT GOVERN THEM AND ARE BANNED IN THE EU ON THE BASIS OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC HEALTH KNOWN IMPACTS

BOBBY: Some of those pesticides were chlorinated pesticides and the results of burning a chlorinated pesticides is that you release dioxins and dioxins persistence.

VO: While these 5 hazardous substances are not banned in South AFrica, Weerts explained the true extent of the damage to the environment and human health is yet to be determined in years to come.

STEVEN: They don't degrade naturally. So they last for fairly long times in the natural environment.

VO: In the meantime, UPL appointed specialist consultants, and testing is underway. Stating no expense or expertise is being spared. Expert cleaning companies dealing with decontaminating the warehouse and river system.

Link: AFTER THE FIRE WAS EXTINGUISHED, THE HEAT WAS ON UPL AND THE AUTHORITIES. NEITHER WERE WILLING TO DO ON-CAMERA INTERVIEWS AND INSTEAD OPTED TO SEND GENERAL WRITTEN STATEMENTS.

VO: Despite agreeing to interviews , eThekwini Municipality and the KZN Department of Economic Development, Tourism and Environmental Affairs sent a joint response stating eThekwini “officials were unaware of its [UPL] existence” prior to the fire. The Municipality is seeking legal guidance on non-compliance with bylaws and monitoring the rehabilitation and remediation efforts following the polluter pays principle.

Neither the municipality nor the provincial government replied to further requests for clarity on permitting and approvals.

While initially open to an on-camera interview, UPL declined after we submitted our list of questions and referred us to two public press statements.

We called the local media co-ordinator Craig Dodds for clarification, he insisted he was not able to speak for UPL.

DODDS: Are you recording this for the purposes of the broadcast //
MAC: yes, we are recording it for the purposes of a broadcast.
DODD: i’ve explained to you i am not a spokesman so there’s really no point for me responding to your questions because I’m not the person to respond to your questions
MAC: Who is their spokesman then? Who is the person that is going to answer for what’s happened?
DODDS:They dont have a spokesman

BOBBY: Corporates don’t want to come out And admit to what they did, what they were doing is wrong. They're going to be a secretive as possible. and that’s corporate’s general approach so there’s no accountability

VO: UPL stated in relation to the MHI or Major Hazardous Installation Regulations, that it took the view that its warehouse operation did not constitute an MHI and that it did not need to conduct a risk assessment. And this view has been confirmed by its legal consultants.

Professor Field has a different legal opinion, she believes the Occupational Health and Safety Act applies in the UPL case, especially in light of the risk that was manifested.

TRACY: If you store substances of a form and quantity that has the potential to cause a major incident and // It's dangerous to the health and safety. Then you require a major hazard, hazardous installation authorization.

VO: Affected residents, like Dr. Ramnarain, are clear that citizens’ rights need to be protected.

MITHA: It's twenty, twenty one allowing a warehouse, a chemical warehouse //to be on our doorstep. We need to make sure that we that this kind of thing doesn't happen again.

BOBBY: Our democracy failed us because those processes were not set in place. we need to be very careful as South Africans to create these economic zones where we break the law purposely to attract foreign direct investment, because foreign direct investment of this sort is what South Africa does not need.

VO: IT’S THE BIGGEST ENVIRONMENTAL DISASTER ARISING FROM THE KZN UNREST. A TORCHED CHEMICAL WAREHOUSE BURNT FOR MORE THAN A WEEK.

CONTAMINATING WATERWAYS, AND COVERING THE SURROUNDING AREAS WITH A BLACK CLOUD OF SMOKE.

MITHA: It was it smelled like something was going to choke me. //C3M2.

VO: WE INVESTIGATE WHAT WENT WRONG AS A COMMUNITY AT RISK DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY.

PROMO 2_ 21 SECONDS
VO: A CHEMICAL STORAGE FACILITY WAS ABLAZE FOR MORE THAN WEEK DURING THE KZN UNREST CAUSING EXTENSIVE ENVIRONMENTAL DAMAGE.

TRACY: The company has not disclosed the exact chemicals and the quantities that were available on that site. //. M7

VO: WE INVESTIGATE WHETHER THE MULTI-NATIONAL COMPANY TICKED ALL THE BOXES WHEN IT CAME TO ENVIRONMENTAL APPROVALS AND PERMITS.

PROMO 3_ 11 SECONDS
VO: A TORCHED CHEMICAL WAREHOUSE BECAME THE TOXIC ECOLOGICAL LEGACY OF THE KZN UNREST - WE ASK WHAT WENT WRONG AS THE DAMAGE TO HUMAN HEALTH AND THE ENVIRONMENT IS YET TO BE DETERMINED?

This can be expected to dissipate rapidly due to normal air movement and precipitation. Air pollution also remains a major concern, as firefighters continue to douse the still smouldering debris. A lot of the gases that people have been breathing in there have been very high in sulphur, that could affect, particularly, people with respiratory illnesses. KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department's Sphume Nowele said - “We are going to be getting those results so that we can make informed decisions in terms of what happens moving forward.” Case Study: Mitha Ramnarain MT EDGECOMBE RESIDENT BOBALO MASIPHULA BLACKBURN RESIDENT Expert: Mr. BOBBY PEEK GROUNDWORK Mr. STEVEN WEERTS SPECIALIST MARINE & ESTUARINE ECOLOGIST Prof. TRACY-LYNN FIELD PROFESSOR OF LAW Mr. CRAIG DODDS UPL COMMS Locations: Durban Hidden Camera: No Legal: Yes Graphics: No Accept / Reject Status: Approved Approved By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk Approval Date: 26 July 2021 Commission Commission Number: 5972 Duration: 10 Delivery Date: Monday, 02 August 2021 Rate: R10100 Accept Contract: I agree with the following CAP Contractual Agreement Legal Viewing: No Accepted By: Nicky Troll Accepted Date: 10 August 2021 Broadcast / Delivery Broadcast: MOD Approved for Broadcast by Editor: Yes, this is approved for broadcast by on 21 June 2026 Approved for Payment: No Insert Details Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Voice-over Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Camera: Duncan Grant Stuart Dodds Sound: Vincent Maphumulo Offline editor: Floris Kotze Online editor: Floris Kotze Audio final mix: Floris Brand Booked Footage Footage returned: No Footage Declaration I confirm that all footage agreements have been signed and submitted via Jotform: No Music Cue Sheet Music Title Type Track Number Duration Publisher Composer Record/CD Number BOLD ACTION 80 00:00:55 KPM CHRISTOPHER TIMOTHY 0957 TIRELESS SEARCH Background 110 00:01:40 KPM MARTYN LEE KENNET 0957 INVESTIGATIONS BEGIN Background 80 00:00:55 SATV THOMAS RICHARD SATVDG 0047 ENTERPRISING Background 60 00:00:57 model THOMAS RICHARD 0018 FORENSIC TRAIL Background 10 00:00:53 KPM CHRISTOPHER TIMOTHY 0957 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 08 August 2021 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 19 August 2021 Script: STRUCTURE VO: The violent riots and looting that ripped through KwaZulu Natal in July, has also triggered extensive environmental damage, following the arson attack on the United Phosphorus Limited, or UPL Chemical warehouse in Cornubia, north of Durban. LINK: IT’S THE BIGGEST ECOLOGICAL DISASTER TO COME OUT OF THE UNPRECEDENTED KZN UNREST. THE SITE WAS ABLAZE FOR 9 DAYS , COVERING THE SURROUNDING AREA IN A THICK BLACK CLOUD OF SMOKE. VO: Babalo Masiphula lives in the informal settlement of Blackburn. BABALO: you can't just breathe bread and as normal as you always it because it's affecting you or your chest VO: He recalls the air pollution was most intense at night, With shacks erected less than 2km from the site. Specialist Anesthesiologist, Dr. Mitha Ramnarain lives about 5 kilometers from the site in Mount Edgecombe. She felt anxious as the clouds of airborne chemicals lingered over her home with ash falling from the sky - as a precaution she kept her children indoors. MITHA: it smelt quite chemical in nature. It was acrid. It was malodorous, would probably be a euphemistic way to describe the odor. It was it smelled like something was going to choke me. VO: UPL, an Indian multinational pesticide and agro-chemicals company – opened Cornubia warehouse in April. It is said to have stored herbicides, pesticide and fungicides – and believed to have contained more than 1500 chemicals that UPL say are overwhelmingly water-based. Fire fighting efforts were hampered with the ongoing unrest straining resources and delaying accessibility to the fire. The roof and surrounding walls collapsed in the intense heat , covering much of the products in metal sheeting and debris. The water used to douse the raging flames, mixed with the exposed chemicals - spilled into the surrounding environment. The effects could be seen in the river, the lagoon, estuary and on the beaches – the water turned a bright turquoise colour and dead fish washed up in affected areas. Beaches were closed, and Blackburn residents were advised not to use the water. BABALO: The water is very bad even now, it's still very bad. //uh, during that week, the water will have changed the color into green. VO: Steven Weerts is a specialist estuarine and marine ecologist. MAC: What did you see the impact of the UPL spill has had? How bad is it? STEVEN: it has pretty much decimated all the aquatic life in that system. VO: Scores of dead marine life were cleared by cleaning companies. These teams are still working on the affected water in the Blackburn area. STEVEN: Those chemical compounds. are designed for agricultural purposes to weed out unwanted things. So they are typically toxic to some elements of wildlife. And obviously in extreme toxicity there's going to be human impact. VO: Residents like, Dr. Ramnarain, were surprised to find out that a chemical storage facility was in such close proximity to residential areas. MITHA: we didn't even know such a factory existed having a chemical warehouse so close to so many conservancies in our area and so many residents, have just left lots of people with no choices and the environment with no choice VO: UPL believes it was appropriately zoned and said in a press release that “the designed fire and containment systems were more than adequate, in ordinary circumstances, to have enabled the facility and the relevant authorities to contain a fire and any associated spillage of product”. Government and City Officials, however, revealed at a press conference not all boxes were ticked by UPL related to approvals and permitting. The onus is on the facility to check what regulations are applicable in order to comply with the laws of that area. UPSOUND PRESS CONFERENCE - BRUCE DALE, SENIOR MANAGER: Ethekwini Municipality 25:36 “They were not in possession of a Scheduled Trade Permit. They did trigger activity, a listing activity in terms of the bylaws. So it's notable there was an aggregation, all of those scheduled activities.” VO: UPL BELIEVES IT WAS FIT FOR PURPOSE. The KZN Provincial Government disclosed that a “specific” environmental impact assessment wasn’t done for the UPL operation. Only an “integrated environmental assessment” was approved for the entire mixed-use development . In terms of a clause in the environmental authorisation a separate EIA would ONLY be required for facilities with storage and handling of dangerous goods that exceed 80m3 in capacity. It’s unclear whether UPL fell into that category or not. The UPL press statement said the company was advised that it did not trigger an environmental assessment under NEMA regulations and that advice has since been confirmed by its legal consultants. VO: The Greater Cornubia mixed-use development project was part of a special national government investment initiative, aimed at attracting investors by prioritizing and fast tracking the normal regulatory processes. Bobby Peek from the environmental justice organisation, GroundWork, believes this created a loophole for companies to bypass some regulations that are intended to prevent harm to human health and the environment. BOBBY: in a normal legal process.. there would have been an emergency response system created for those that could have been impacted upon if something went wrong at this facility. None of that took place. VO: South African legislation ensures the rights of citizens to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being is protected, explains Professor of Law, Tracy-Lynn Field. TRACY: // The problem with deciding whether those laws apply is that we don't know. We haven't been given the information. The company has not disclosed the exact chemicals and the quantities that were available on that site. VO: Initially, even the authorities were not given a complete inventory by UPL , subsequently it has been supplied, but not made public. TRACY: What would be a reasonable and justifiable limitation of the right to information in this instance? // I can't think of a good reason. LINK: GROUNDWORK HAS SEEN THE INVENTORY OF SOME OF THE CHEMICALS THAT WERE STORED AT THE WAREHOUSE. AND OF THOSE 5 ARE CLASSIFIED AS HIGHLY HAZARDOUS PESTICIDES BY THE United Nations BODIES THAT GOVERN THEM AND ARE BANNED IN THE EU ON THE BASIS OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC HEALTH KNOWN IMPACTS BOBBY: Some of those pesticides were chlorinated pesticides and the results of burning a chlorinated pesticides is that you release dioxins and dioxins persistence. VO: While these 5 hazardous substances are not banned in South AFrica, Weerts explained the true extent of the damage to the environment and human health is yet to be determined in years to come. STEVEN: They don't degrade naturally. So they last for fairly long times in the natural environment. VO: In the meantime, UPL appointed specialist consultants, and testing is underway. Stating no expense or expertise is being spared. Expert cleaning companies dealing with decontaminating the warehouse and river system. Link: AFTER THE FIRE WAS EXTINGUISHED, THE HEAT WAS ON UPL AND THE AUTHORITIES. NEITHER WERE WILLING TO DO ON-CAMERA INTERVIEWS AND INSTEAD OPTED TO SEND GENERAL WRITTEN STATEMENTS. VO: Despite agreeing to interviews , eThekwini Municipality and the KZN Department of Economic Development, Tourism and Environmental Affairs sent a joint response stating eThekwini “officials were unaware of its [UPL] existence” prior to the fire. The Municipality is seeking legal guidance on non-compliance with bylaws and monitoring the rehabilitation and remediation efforts following the polluter pays principle. Neither the municipality nor the provincial government replied to further requests for clarity on permitting and approvals. While initially open to an on-camera interview, UPL declined after we submitted our list of questions and referred us to two public press statements. We called the local media co-ordinator Craig Dodds for clarification, he insisted he was not able to speak for UPL. DODDS: Are you recording this for the purposes of the broadcast // MAC: yes, we are recording it for the purposes of a broadcast. DODD: i’ve explained to you i am not a spokesman so there’s really no point for me responding to your questions because I’m not the person to respond to your questions MAC: Who is their spokesman then? Who is the person that is going to answer for what’s happened? DODDS:They dont have a spokesman BOBBY: Corporates don’t want to come out And admit to what they did, what they were doing is wrong. They're going to be a secretive as possible. and that’s corporate’s general approach so there’s no accountability VO: UPL stated in relation to the MHI or Major Hazardous Installation Regulations, that it took the view that its warehouse operation did not constitute an MHI and that it did not need to conduct a risk assessment. And this view has been confirmed by its legal consultants. Professor Field has a different legal opinion, she believes the Occupational Health and Safety Act applies in the UPL case, especially in light of the risk that was manifested. TRACY: If you store substances of a form and quantity that has the potential to cause a major incident and // It's dangerous to the health and safety. Then you require a major hazard, hazardous installation authorization. VO: Affected residents, like Dr. Ramnarain, are clear that citizens’ rights need to be protected. MITHA: It's twenty, twenty one allowing a warehouse, a chemical warehouse //to be on our doorstep. We need to make sure that we that this kind of thing doesn't happen again. BOBBY: Our democracy failed us because those processes were not set in place. we need to be very careful as South Africans to create these economic zones where we break the law purposely to attract foreign direct investment, because foreign direct investment of this sort is what South Africa does not need. CONTAMINATING WATERWAYS, AND COVERING THE SURROUNDING AREAS WITH A BLACK CLOUD OF SMOKE. MITHA: It was it smelled like something was going to choke me. //C3M2. VO: WE INVESTIGATE WHAT WENT WRONG AS A COMMUNITY AT RISK DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY. PROMO 2_ 21 SECONDS VO: A CHEMICAL STORAGE FACILITY WAS ABLAZE FOR MORE THAN WEEK DURING THE KZN UNREST CAUSING EXTENSIVE ENVIRONMENTAL DAMAGE. TRACY: The company has not disclosed the exact chemicals and the quantities that were available on that site. //. M7 VO: WE INVESTIGATE WHETHER THE MULTI-NATIONAL COMPANY TICKED ALL THE BOXES WHEN IT CAME TO ENVIRONMENTAL APPROVALS AND PERMITS. PROMO 3_ 11 SECONDS VO: A TORCHED CHEMICAL WAREHOUSE BECAME THE TOXIC ECOLOGICAL LEGACY OF THE KZN UNREST - WE ASK WHAT WENT WRONG AS THE DAMAGE TO HUMAN HEALTH AND THE ENVIRONMENT IS YET TO BE DETERMINED?

metadata.Summary: The arson attack on the United Phosphorus Limited (UPL)Chemical factory is the biggest environmental disaster arising from the KZN unrest. The building north of Durban burned for days, taking firefighters more than a week to douse the flames - the damage is not confined to the facility. Smoke blanketed the north of Durban and rivers, lagoons and beaches all the way up to the North Coast were contaminated. The fire was finally extinguished by 5pm on Thursday. Unanswered questions around the approval of the factory that opened in April this year have local residents and environmental activists up in arms as the extent of the damage to the environment and the human life is yet to be determined.
metadata.Further information: The UPL warehouse in Cornubia, which housed 1600 hazardous herbicides, fungicides and pesticides, was targeted Monday 12 July by looters. The Indian multinational pesticide company United Phosphorus Limited (UPL)’s Chemical Plant in Cornubia, Durban is situated near the uMhlanga lagoon and the Ohlanga River, which feeds into the Indian Ocean. ACCORDING TO ETHEKWINI MUNICIPALITY UPL NEVER APPLIED FOR A PERMIT TO STORE HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS THAT HAD AFFECTED AIR AND WATER. Sabelo Ngcobo, director for impact management and coastal management at the provincial level, responding to a question about the environmental impact assessment, said one developer for the area had applied for everything to be undertaken. "It was not specific to UPL. It was registered for residential, logistics, commercial and light industrial use. UPL was authorised within that authority. We still need to determine whether they were compliant." WHAT WENT UP IN FLAME The plant housed hundreds of hazardous herbicides, fungicides and pesticides. It only opened it’s doors at this site in April 2021 – just four months before the blaze. It took firefighters more than a week to douse the flames and the damage was not confined to the facility. A complete list of the volume and types of pesticides and other poisonous products that were set on fire has yet to be disclosed publicly as this might “create unnecessary anxiety”, the company suggested earlier this week. Though it remains unclear what exactly was in the warehouse at the time of the fire, the Indian agrochemicals chemicals giant UPL markets a wide range of highly toxic formulations on its South African website including 52 insecticides, 124 herbicides, 43 fungicides, rat poison, fumigants and other poisonous compounds — notably 2,4-D, glyphosate, paraquat, chlorophenoxy, triclopyrbutoxy ethel esters, atrazine, carbofuran, cyanamide and chlorpyrifos. eThekwini Fire Department Divisional Commander Bruce de Gier noted that the warehouse caved in and collapsed within the space of about an hour after a massive fireball explosion tore through the roof of the warehouse, ripping the overhead sprinkler systems and water pipes out of the walls and roof. The remains of smouldering chemical drums and canisters were now covered by tons of metal sheeting, steel beams, brick and concrete debris, making it impossible to douse the fire completely. “The fireball went through the roof in front of our eyes. The building was completely destroyed. It looks like Hiroshima inside there now.” KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department's Sphume Nowele described the levels of toxicity after the chemical spillage and air pollution in parts of the province: “It is serious, and it should not be underestimated in any way.” BUT WAS THE PLANT DODGE TO START WITH? Further concerns have also been raised about why a major storage facility housing hazardous and toxic chemicals did not have bunding to contain the deadly overflow into the environment. Bunds are similar to large concrete moats that are designed to capture and contain effluent overflow and pollution – even in the event of heavy rainfall and the large volumes of water often used to fight fires. Senior manager for pollution control in eThekwini Metro, Bruce Dale, said there was also no Major Hazard Installation (MHI). In occupational health terms, an MHI ensures the quantity of any substance that has the potential to cause a major incident is kept. "Unfortunately, it does not appear there was any Major Hazard Installation application made and unfortunately local government, we are not aware and it was not brought to our attention that there was a storage facility there. "If it was brought to our attention, we know there are sensitive receptors downstream including the sea, estuary and shopping centres. Unfortunately, we are not aware of any MHI application otherwise they would have brought it to the attention of the municipality and we would have had to look at mitigation measures to prevent any explosions or impact on the environment in terms of air quality and water quality impacts." It appears that UPL does not have an approved Environmental Management Plan in place, as it has submitted a plan but has not received approval yet – by the company’s own admittance – “the plan became somewhat academic due to the extraordinary circumstances which could not have been foreseen, notably the civil unrest which resulted in the looting and arson and barricading of access routes which resulted in the long delay in the fire department and other response services being able to access the site.” NOTE! THE PLANT OPENED 4 MONTHS BEFORE THE LOOTING Siphumelele Nowele, chief director of environmental management at the department, said that if it was deliberately hidden from them that highly toxic substances were stored there, there were processes to follow that could lead to criminal action. "But we can't jump to that point until we know." From a waste management point of view, because the kind of chemicals at UPL were highly hazardous, they should not be disposed of at a landfill site without provincial consent. ENVIRONMENTAL AND HEALTH IMPACTS The pollution from the days-long burning fire at the UPL chemical plant resulted in dead fish washing ashore because of toxins from the Umhlanga lagoon. While the KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department has started running tests and evaluating the damage to the environment, an additional team of specialists in aquatic systems, epidemiology, waste and pollution as well as oceans and coasts compliance will provide support. BEACHES & BUSINESSES CLOSED Beaches in the vicinity remain closed to the public and while some businesses are desperate to reopen, they’ve been advised that this was not safe, as the damage and its costs were evaluated. Oceanographer Lisa Gaustella estimates that the lagoon would take “maybe a year or two” to recover, starting with organisms that live there and in the ocean.“In the upper reaches, smaller animals like frogs, which are a good indicator of wetland health, will take longer.” HEALTH IMPACT There had been "numerous complaints" through emergency services regarding air quality. Residents in both nearby residential estates and informal settlements have been affected. Some people have evacuated their homes; others have had to undergo medical treatment for respiratory problems and nausea. ** HAVE A LONG LIST OF CASE STUDIES WILLING TO GO ON CAMERA Reggie Govender, a doctor based in Somerset Park, confirmed “About five patients a day have been coming in for the past week - it has mainly affected chronic sinusitis and asthmatic patients but even people without these are also complaining,” Rory Macpherson, the local councillor for Mount Edgecombe/Umhlanga who visited the beach near the Ohlanga River mouth said “This estuary is dead, dead, dead … and the sea and coastline have also been poisoned”. Macpherson also drove to Cornubia earlier last week and discovered that polluted bright blue water was still flowing out of a broken stormwater drain some distance from the warehouse alongside a stream that leads into the Ohlanga River. Local civil society groups have also issued an “urgent but unofficial public health warning” cautioning people in the vicinity to stay indoors and to consider moving vulnerable people out of the area for the next few days. “As far as is possible, stay indoors as much as you can, with windows closed, particularly if your home is in the direction of the chemical plume. If you, your child, or elderly people with chronic chest and heart disease live in the area of the smoke, and it is at all possible to stay with relatives outside the area for the next few days, then it is advisable to do so,” according to a press statement signed by among others, Prof Rajen Naidoo, head of Occupational and Environmental Health at the University of KwaZulu-Natal. According to UPL, Verdoorn had indicated that some of the herbicides, such as acetochlor, metolachlor, phenoxy carboxylic acids (2,4-D, MCPA and benzoic acids, or dicamba) may not have burnt out completely: “Two pyrethroids — alpha-cypermethrin and lambda-cyhalothrin — which are dermal, eye and respiratory tract irritants may have been present in the smoke. These chemicals were suspended in the atmosphere and have precipitated since the fire, more noticeably during the late night and early hours of the morning, resulting in an acrid smell. “Combined with the smoke inhalation, this may cause drying out of the mucous membranes in the nasal tract and some mild bleeding, especially when blowing the nose. It may also cause discomfort in the oesophagus and trachea. “However as the fire is being doused, the release of these substances into the atmosphere diminishes. This can be expected to dissipate rapidly due to normal air movement and precipitation. SPECIALIST TESTING UNDERWAY Specialists in marine biology, water, air, chemicals, estuaries and others were still awaiting test results to determine the severity of the pollution. Air pollution also remains a major concern, as firefighters continue to douse the still smouldering debris. A lot of the gases that people have been breathing in there have been very high in sulphur, that could affect, particularly, people with respiratory illnesses. KwaZulu-Natal Environmental Affairs Department's Sphume Nowele said - “We are going to be getting those results so that we can make informed decisions in terms of what happens moving forward.”
